title: Angevin Empire
capsule: The Angevin Empire was the cross-Channel conglomerate of territories held by the Plantagenet dynasty, assembled when Henry II — already count of Anjou and duke of Normandy — became King of England in 1154 and through his wife Eleanor of Aquitaine controlled Gascony and Poitou, giving the dynasty more French land than the Capetian king himself held. The realm stretched from the Pyrenees to the Scottish border and extended into Ireland after 1171, but it functioned as a personal union rather than a unified state and depended on constant royal itineration. King John lost Normandy and most of the Loire territories to Philip II Augustus of France between 1202 and 1204 at Château Gaillard and Rouen; by the end of his reign only Gascony remained, ending the empire as a coherent entity.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The outer bounds of the empire are well documented through royal charters and chroniclers; the internal division of administrative authority between English and French institutions makes territorial representation inherently schematic.
